name: Slowed and reverb looksmaxxing edits

card.summary: Short video edits that set before-and-after or face clips to slowed, echoey music, the sound style used to give transformation and "ascension" clips an atmospheric mood.

quick.overview:
Slowed and reverb is a remixing technique that slows a song and adds reverb. In looksmaxxing communities it is the typical soundtrack to viral face and glow-up edits.

It does not change a person's looks itself; it frames how transformations and faces are shown online.
quick.how: Creators pair slowed, reverberant tracks with clips, often using free editors such as Audacity for the audio [1].
quick.risks: No physical risks. Houston music writers have criticised the style as a diluted version of chopped and screwed [1].

lead: Slowed and reverb is an internet remix style that slows down an existing song and adds reverb, usually with free audio editors, and derives from chopped and screwed hip-hop [1][2]. In looksmaxxing culture it is the audio style often attached to viral face, glow-up and "mogging" clips.

The style grew in 2017 when Houston producer Jarylun Moore, known as slater!, posted slowed and reverb remixes on YouTube, and later spread to TikTok and Spotify [1]. Chopped and screwed was pioneered in early-1990s Houston by DJ Screw [2].

chain: Transformations and faces presented more dramatically
angle.text: The audio does not alter appearance; creators use it to present faces and before-and-after clips with a more dramatic mood.

paras: Chopped and screwed began with DJ Screw in Houston in the early 1990s and spread through DJs such as Michael "5000" Watts and OG Ron C [2]. Slowed and reverb became common on YouTube after 2017, often with looping anime clips [1]. Pitchfork covered its rise in April 2020 [1].
In 2020 a viral TikTok that did not credit chopped and screwed prompted critics to call slowed and reverb a gentrified version of the Houston style [1].

timeline.event: DJ Screw pioneers chopped and screwed in Houston [2].
slater! popularizes slowed and reverb on YouTube [1].
Pitchfork covers the trend; TikTok backlash [1].
